source.title: Size Doesn't Matter: Cosine-Scored Sparse Autoencoders

record.file_problem: None; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study measures sparse-feature recovery in LLMs and compares SAE dictionaries, including evidence that strict feature overlap is low across scoring methods. This refines evidence for SAE features as canonical units; it does not test toy-model superposition itself.
record.gate_note: Rows cover sparse-probing results and cross-dictionary feature overlap, which bear on SAE recoverability and canonicality. The paper also reports reconstruction, KL/CE preservation, ablations, steering, and architecture diagnostics; those results do not directly measure the listed claim versions and are omitted. Values used to select settings and results cited from other work are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: The paper is mainly an SAE architecture study comparing cosine-scored and inner-product encoders. Its probing results measure its own method against a baseline, not whether LLMs contain recoverable sparse features, so they do not test V4. However, its cross-dictionary overlap analyses do bear on V5. Dictionaries trained on the same Qwen3-8B layer, differing only in encoder score, share few features under strict matching. Most standard-SAE slots hold norm-conditioned features the model does not read. This argues that SAE features are not canonical units independent of training choices.
record.authors_conclusion: Partly right. The authors conclude that inner-product scoring is the wrong default for SAEs on normalized residual streams, and that cosine scoring should be the default. At matched reconstruction and per-feature interpretability, cosine scoring yields more concept-aligned features. Most of the gain comes from features the standard SAE never learns, because its slots go to norm detectors. The gain is distributional rather than better per-feature legibility. The authors only briefly note that dictionaries differ across architectures, consistent with non-canonicality (citing Leask et al.); this is not their main conclusion.
record.recipe_differences: The paper trains cosine-scored versus inner-product SAEs on transformer residual streams and evaluates probing and dictionary overlap; it does not reproduce the original toy-network superposition method.
record.method_sensitivity: Sparse-probing gains vary by dataset (sentiment is the exception), layer, and model family/size. The paper reports different overlap rates under loose versus strict matching criteria. Its main probing results use Qwen3-8B L18, 500M tokens, and three SAE-training seeds; the per-dataset breakdown is reported at one representative seed.

fits_no_version.finding: Changing only the SAE encoder score from inner product to cosine raises single-feature sparse-probing top-1 on Qwen3-8B L18 from 0.667 to 0.813. The gain is smaller on Gemma-2-2B (+3.4%) and reverses on sentiment and at deep LayerNorm layers.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Which concept-aligned features an SAE recovers depends strongly on encoder scoring geometry relative to the model's normalization.

record.peer_reviewed: Spotlight paper at the ICML 2026 Workshop on Mechanistic Interpretability; also listed as arXiv.org.
record.problems: No ground-truth feature inventory is used to establish dictionary completeness. The cross-dictionary overlap results compare scoring methods rather than establishing stability across repeated seeds; one strict-identity report uses only n = 3–6 paired features. Most cross-model checks are smaller-budget, and the per-dataset breakdown is single-seed. The paper states that its evaluation is English-focused and covers models no larger than 8B.
record.rows_left_out: Omitted additional probing metrics (top-2/top-5), further layers and model-size sweeps, and related SAE ablations because the retained rows cover the tested sparse-feature-recovery and dictionary-overlap findings; omitted reconstruction and intervention results because those do not directly test V4 or V5.

untested.parts: No toy models, sparsity transition or feature geometry.
No neuron-level polysemanticity or capacity-allocation analysis.
No analysis of the causes of neuron polysemanticity.
SAEs are used as a tool. The study does not test whether features are spread across neurons or whether sparse features exist in the model, as opposed to being SAE artifacts.
Completeness against ground truth, and stability across SAE training seeds (dictionary overlap across seeds is not reported).
No test of one-dimensional versus multi-dimensional features.

missing.what: Matched-feature count: 8,661 of 64,450 alive standard features (13.4%) match a cosine feature (activation correlation ≥0.7 and decoder cosine >0.7). The remaining 55,789 fire mainly on high-norm tokens (86% of activations in Q4).
missing.locator: §4.3; Appendix G 'Unmatched features by norm quartile'

missing.what: Decoder direction overlap: >0.7 cosine match for only 31% of 1000 sampled features, which conflicts with the 73–78% mutual-nearest-neighbour figure.
Post-hoc cosine scoring of a trained standard SAE overlaps <11% (Jaccard 10.6%) with a from-scratch cosine dictionary. A score swap moves probing to match the read-time score.

record.verdict_notes: The probing rows are own-method versus baseline comparisons and were relinked to none. The V5 evidence compares encoder variants rather than seeds, so it speaks to dependence on a training choice. Seed stability is untested; the paper flags a cross-seed analysis as needed. The Leask et al. non-canonicality result is cited, not tested here.

versions.untested_parts: No toy networks or feature-overlap geometry with more sparse features than dimensions are tested.
Does not test neuron polysemanticity, dedicated neuron capacity, or competition among model features for neuron dimensions.
Does not test polysemantic neurons or alternative causes of neuron polysemanticity.

Tests SAE-recovered sparse features using probing on selected English-language datasets and model settings; does not test feature spreading across neurons or broad multilingual, instruction-tuned, or RLHF coverage.
Compares SAE feature dictionaries across scoring methods, but does not establish completeness against ground-truth features or stability across repeated training seeds.
Does not test whether model features are one-dimensional versus multidimensional.

relationships.condition: Qwen3-8B L18 standard vs cosine-scored SAE dictionaries (same data, layer and recipe; only the encoder score differs), strict matching
relationships.reason: Strict overlap is 6–17% (r16) and below 1% in the alive-paired subset (r17). Only 8,661 of 64,450 standard features match under correlation and cosine >0.7 criteria, and 55,789 standard-only features track token norm (text, §4.3). The dictionary depends on a scoring choice.
relationships.display_finding: Strict overlap was 6–17%, and below 1% in the alive-paired subset. Only 8,661 of 64,450 standard features matched under correlation and cosine > 0.7 criteria, and 55,789 standard-only features tracked token norm, so the dictionary depended on the scoring choice.

source_check.reason: r16 reports only 6–17% strict overlap; r17 explicitly reports <1% for the alive-and-paired subset, although its n qualifier is unexplained. These results contradict a recipe-independent canonical inventory.

relationships.condition: Same dictionaries under loose mutual-nearest-neighbour matching

relationships.display_finding: Loose decoder-direction matching reached 73–78%, while the paper reports 31% at cosine >0.7, so apparent overlap depended on the criterion.
